title: QOS / Session Surge & Timeout Walkthrough - BrightCart
summary: Redwood AE + SE ran an edge-case demo for BrightCart focused on very long conversation contexts, bursty TPS, and streaming backpressure/timeouts. The call covered routing fallbacks, KV cache eviction behavior, console dashboards for latency SLOs, and Optimize suggestions (batching/quantization). Customer raised concerns about PCI/compliance, regional failover, and canary rollouts. Agreed next steps: run a short pilot with sample workload, share security SOC artifacts, and schedule a follow-up benchmark run with BrightCart traffic trace.
next_steps: Redwood to share SOC2 summary and KMS integration notes (Lena)
BrightCart to export 24h traffic trace for pilot (Omar)
action_items: Lena Park: send SOC2 + security one-pager by 2026-11-23
Diego Morales: provide sample conf for streaming timeouts and fallback policy by 2026-11-25
Omar Alvi: upload anonymized 24h traffic trace before pilot start
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-19 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Arnav Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (BrightCart CTO), Omar Alvi (BrightCart Platform), Jen Park (BrightCart SRE), Tariq Hassan (BrightCart PM)

[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
[00:08] Maya Singh: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks, Lena.
[00:12] Lena Park: Cool. Quick agenda, we'll do a targeted demo on session surge behavior with very long histories, show how streaming backpressure can be surfaced and mitigated, then walk the console Optimize suggestions. Diego will drive the technical bits.
[00:22] Diego Morales: Hi all. I'll start with a short runbook: show a synthetic long-context chat (50k tokens), then kick off a TPS surge to emulate checkout season, and demonstrate timeouts and automatic fallbacks. A note — some terms in our infra sometimes come out as "K-V cash" in logs so ignore the audio tangle there.
[00:35] Omar Alvi: Quick context from our side — BrightCart uses a mix of hosted endpoints and a self-hosted redis cache for user histories, we want to push to 3k TPS during checkout windows but retain last 200 messages per session. Concerned about latency spikes and cost.
[00:50] Diego Morales: Perfect. Two immediate knobs: 1) KV cache retention/eviction policy (we call it KV cache in the console), 2) routing policy — you can route to cheaper quantized variants under load. We'll show both.
[01:15] Arnav Patel: Also we'll point out the console trace where you can see prefix-cache hits vs misses, and the per-token cost delta when Quant1 vs Float16 is selected.

[05:02] Demo start. Diego screenshares a terminal and Redwood Console.
[05:09] Diego Morales: Starting the long-context generator — this sim creates a 50k token synthetic history compiled from product listings and prior carts. Note: synthetic tends to have odd tokenization, so timings vary.
[05:35] [screen noise]
[05:38] Jen Park: It's interesting that you can push that many tokens into a single session, our current infra truncates at 10k tokens, any best practices?
[05:45] Diego Morales: Right, two approaches: progressive summarization or prefix-maintained KV cache where we store compressed embeddings for earlier messages. Redwood supports both; Optimize will recommend summarization thresholds based on the traffic trace.
[06:10] Diego Morales: Kicking the surge simulator now — ramping from 200 TPS to 3k TPS over 90s.
[06:22] [simulated load increases, console graphs spike]
[06:33] Omar Alvi: Whoa, I see latency creeping.
[06:36] Diego Morales: Yep, so first thing that happens is batch buildup causing larger GPU kernels to be selected, which can increase p99. Our runtime then considers fallbacks if latency SLO is breached.
[06:50] [automated fallback log appears]
[06:52] Arnav Patel: Here's a fallback — policy routed some requests to a quantized-compatible variant. Note the transcript shows "quant one" but sometimes the transcript writes it as "q one" — small ASR thing.
[07:12] Maya Singh: Does that change output quality? We can't have hallucinations in checkout flows.
[07:18] Diego Morales: Good question. In many cases a carefully-tuned quantized variant preserves correctness for instruction-following tasks. For strict checkout canonicalization we suggest a canary: route a small percentage (5-10%) to quantized first and run similarity/regression checks. We also keep the float variant available for fallthrough.

[12:10] Streaming backpressure scenario.
[12:15] Diego Morales: Now enabling streaming with token-level flushes. When the serving queue saturates, you'll see stall markers in the stream — those show up in the console as chunk delays and in the client as longer chunk intervals.
[12:34] Jen Park: If a chunk stalls do we drop it or wait? Our client can't block for more than 2s per chunk.
[12:40] Diego Morales: Redwood supports configurable chunk timeouts. If a chunk exceeds the per-chunk timeout, the runtime will attempt to send a graceful partial response and flag the request for a fast fallback route. There's a trade: aggressive timeouts reduce p99 but can yield trimmed outputs.
[13:10] [simulated 2s chunk timeout triggers, partial output returned]
[13:18] Omar Alvi: We saw a partial address field trimmed — that's risky for our use.
[13:22] Arnav Patel: For structured outputs, enable enforced schemas + function/tool calling; these can trigger automatic retries for missing fields rather than naive truncation. We'll demo that next.

[19:02] Function-calling and structured output demo.
[19:10] Diego Morales: Turning on structured mode — requests will attempt to emit JSON. When streaming stalls, the SDK can re-request the remainder via a short re-issue with the same session KV, which is cheaper than a full re-run. Note, re-issuing depends on preserved KV cache and session affinity — if your session migrates to another host and the KV isn't replicated, you'll see a cold restart.
[19:46] Maya Singh: How does that interact with Dedicated vs Hosted? We want session guarantees for PCI conversations.
[19:55] Lena Park: Dedicated gives stronger session locality guarantees and you can pin models/hosts for higher affinity. Hosted provides cross-region failover but you need to configure cache replication for strict locality.

[26:00] Timeout and graceful degradation playbook.
[26:08] Diego Morales: Our recommended playbook: 1) set per-chunk timeout at client (e.g., 2s) 2) set server-side streaming timeout slightly higher (3-4s) to allow for retry window 3) activate fallback policy to quant variant at 1% then ramp to 20% if SLOs breach 4) use Optimize to get suggested batching and kv retention values.
[26:42] Jen Park: Do you have concrete numbers for batching tradeoffs?
[26:45] Diego Morales: Example: small responses, batch size 4-8 yields best latency/cost; long-context with big KV hits we often lower batch window to 10-20ms to reduce p99. Optimize will analyze token distribution and suggest both a batch target and a coalescing window.

[33:50] Live console: telemetry & Optimize suggestions.
[33:58] Diego Morales: Here's the Optimize tab — it picked up our simulated traffic and recommended: increase prefix cache retention to 10k tokens (for your use), set quant fallback ramp to 5% initial, and for long sessions enable incremental summarization after 30k tokens.
[34:25] Maya Singh: That prefix retention seems high — storage and privacy implications?
[34:30] Lena Park: You control retention. For PCI data you'd likely apply redaction policies and keep only embeddings or hashes for older turns. We have KMS integrations and audit logs; we'll share the SOC2 docs.

[40:10] Canary and rollouts.
[40:16] Arnav Patel: For rollouts we demonstrated canary routing — you can route by user cohort or by request fingerprint. If a canary triggers metric regressions, automatic rollback can be configured.
[40:40] Tariq Hassan: For us, important to test rollouts against A/B of quality metrics not just latency. How do you wire that?
[40:47] Diego Morales: We instrument regression checks that run prompt sets and similarity thresholds. For structured checkout flows we recommend automated unit tests in the pipeline. Console shows diffs and alerts on divergence.

[46:00] Failure mode: cold KV eviction during migration.
[46:08] Diego Morales: We simulated a host migration where KV wasn't replicated — result was a cold restart and full context re-hydration adding ~300-400ms tail latency. In our logs that showed as repeated "kv miss" lines (sometimes transcribed as "K V miss" or "K-V cash miss").
[46:33] Jen Park: How to prevent that?
[46:36] Diego Morales: Enable cross-host KV replication or use sticky sessions on Dedicated. Also configure fallback to a summarized context if KV cold miss occurs.

[51:20] Customer questions and clarifications.
[51:25] Maya Singh: Can you show the exact timeout parameters to put in our SDK?
[51:30] Diego Morales: Sure. I'll paste a snippet after the call; quick version: client_chunk_timeout_ms=2000, server_chunk_timeout_ms=3500, request_retry_budget=2, fallback_ramp_plan=[1,5,20].
[51:50] Omar Alvi: For the pilot, we want a run with our real traffic for 24h and compare p50/p95/p99 and cost delta.
[51:58] Lena Park: We'll do that. Diego, we'll need a runner config.
[52:05] Diego Morales: I'll prepare a runner config and an Optimize export that includes suggested quantization levels and batching windows.

[55:10] Recap and next steps.
[55:15] Lena Park: Recap — send SOC2 and KMS notes, Diego will send timeout and runner config, BrightCart to share anonymized trace, schedule pilot kickoff week of 11/29.
[55:30] Maya Singh: Sounds good, thank you.
[55:34] Jen Park: Appreciate the structured output demo.
[55:40] Lena Park: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with links.
[55:46] [meeting ends, brief hold music on some lines]

Notes on transcription: occasional ASR mislabels for product names (e.g., "Optimize" sometimes appears as "opt eyes"), and speaker turns sometimes show "Speaker 3" in the raw export; cleaned here for readability but some original verbatim markers remain.
